meta.title: SEO linter for Nuxt and CI
meta.description: A Nuxt module, a DevTools tab and a CI crawler that fails the pipeline on SEO regressions. Any stack, 42 rules, open source.

hero.lead: A Nuxt module, a DevTools tab and a CI crawler that fails the pipeline on SEO regressions. Any stack.

term.context: ranklint diff, demo app in this repo

pillars.title: A linter, not a score out of 100
pillars.lead: Ranklint reads the HTML your server actually returns to a crawler and names the exact problem: an empty title, a broken canonical, a heading hierarchy that skips a level, a one-way hreflang pair. Three surfaces, one set of rules.

module.title: Nuxt module
module.text: sitemap.xml, robots.txt and typed JSON-LD out of the box. One command to install, no config required.

devtools.title: DevTools tab
devtools.text: Issues, heading structure and meta tags for the current route — right on the dev server, while you write code.

cli.title: CI crawler
cli.text: Crawls your deployed site through Chromium. Works with any stack — Nuxt not required.

devtools.title: Visible on the dev server, not a month later
devtools.lead: The SEO tab in Nuxt DevTools shows the current route the way a crawler sees it: the list of issues, the heading tree and every meta tag. It refreshes when the host page navigates and when the DOM changes, and there is a Rescan button.
devtools.b1: Every finding carries a selector and a suggestion on how to fix it
devtools.b2: {count} of the {total} rules need no network, with the same ids and levels as in CI
devtools.b3: JSON-LD is validated in dev: warnings land in the console and in the panel

panel.t1: Heading jump fixture main heading here

rules.title: {total} rules, {groups} categories
rules.leadPre: Every rule has an id and a level:
rules.leadPost: Levels live in a config file next to your code, not in somebody's head.
rules.configNote: levels are overridden just like in ESLint

cat.headings: h1 length, a single h1, empty headings, skipped levels
cat.http: mixed content, soft 404, TTFB budget, x-robots, viewport
cat.i18n: hreflang: symmetry, valid targets, locale leaks
cat.images: alt text, explicit dimensions, lazy loading above the fold
cat.indexability: content in SSR, a reachable sitemap, noindex in the sitemap
cat.links: broken links, orphan pages, redirect chains, trailing slash
cat.robots: policy per environment, expected disallow, reachability, declared sitemap, zones not blocked
cat.structured-data: JSON-LD that parses, required Schema.org fields

ci.leadPre: A quarterly crawl turns into a backlog everyone forgets. Ranklint checks every pull request:
ci.leadPost: compares it against the base branch and fails the pipeline only on new errors. Existing debt never blocks a merge.
ci.note: Pre-existing findings are flagged in the report but never fail the build.

formats.title: Report formats
formats.note: junit goes into your runner's reports, gitlab is a Code Quality report, and github turns every finding into a pull request annotation.

steps.title: Two steps in the pipeline
steps.note: Code review misses SEO regressions — in a browser everything looks fine. The exit code doesn't.

stack.title: Nuxt is optional
stack.lead: The crawler speaks HTTP and renders pages in Chromium through Playwright. It does not care what serves them — Next, Django, WordPress or static files on a CDN.
stack.zonesNote: Each zone has its own list of checks and an owner: a zone you own is crawled in full, an external one only gets a HEAD check on the links that point at it.
stack.b1: Profiles gate the slow work: Lighthouse on release, a plain audit on every pull request
stack.b2: The Lighthouse profile plugs in as a separate check
stack.b3: Custom rules are plain functions that live in your repository
stack.b4: An HTML report with grouped findings — for people who live outside the terminal

monitor.title: Checking does not stop at deploy
monitor.leadPost: run crawls production on a schedule, keeps every report in history and tells you when something breaks.

crux.title: CrUX field data
crux.text: Real-user LCP, CLS and INP for the whole origin land next to the linter's findings in the same report.

gsc.title: Search Console
gsc.text: URL Inspection reports Google's indexing verdict, the coverage state and rich-results issues for the first ten pages of the crawl.

alerts.title: Alerts and history
alerts.text: A Slack or Telegram message on every new error; the report history lives on GitHub or GitLab Pages.

seotext.title: What is an SEO linter
seotext.lead: An SEO linter reads the HTML your site actually returns and reports the things that cost you traffic: a missing title, a canonical pointing at a redirect, a heading level that jumps from h1 to h3, a hreflang pair that only links one way. It is the same idea as ESLint, applied to the markup search engines read instead of the JavaScript you ship.
seotext.quote: The exit code makes the decision instead of a person.

ci.title: SEO audit in CI, not in a spreadsheet
ci.text: Most SEO work dies in a spreadsheet. Someone runs a crawler once a quarter, exports a list of 400 issues, and the list rots while the site keeps shipping. A linter inverts that: the crawl runs on every pull request, the report is a diff, and the only thing you have to look at is what changed since the last green build. ranklint stores the JSON report as a build artifact, compares the current run against it and posts the difference as a comment.
ci.link: See how audit and diff fit together

regressions.title: SEO regression testing on every pull request
regressions.text: Regressions are rarely dramatic. A refactor drops the canonical from one template, a CMS migration leaves 40 pages without a description, an experiment adds noindex and nobody removes it. Those changes pass code review because nothing looks broken in the browser. A crawl that runs with your tests catches them in the same hour they were introduced. Severity is per rule, so title length can stay a warning while a missing canonical stops the merge.

module.title: Nuxt SEO module with zero config
module.text: In a Nuxt 4 app the module covers the parts that are pure plumbing. It serves sitemap.xml from your routes, robots.txt that knows the difference between staging and production, and JSON-LD that is validated against Schema.org while you develop, so a broken Product or FAQPage block shows up as a console warning instead of a silent loss of rich results. Each block is opt out, and a disabled block is never registered, so it costs nothing at runtime.

stack.title: Any stack: crawl a deployed site
stack.text: The crawler talks HTTP, not framework internals. Point it at a URL and it renders each page in Chromium, which means client rendered content is judged the way a search engine judges it, and pages that only exist after hydration are reported as an indexing problem. One domain can be split into zones when different apps live under different paths, and profiles keep the slow checks off the fast pipeline.

lighthouse.q: How is this different from Lighthouse?
lighthouse.a: Lighthouse gives a page a score. Ranklint crawls the whole site and returns a list of concrete rules with ids and levels — something you can fail a build on and diff between branches.

nuxtseo.aPost: what was actually served — and does it in CI as well. They don't conflict.

nonnuxt.q: We're not on Nuxt. Will it work?
nonnuxt.a: Yes. The CLI crawler works over HTTP against any deployed site. Without Nuxt you only lose the module and the DevTools tab.

pipeline.q: Won't this start failing every build?
pipeline.aPost: is for: it fails a build only on errors that are new relative to the base branch, while a bare audit exits 1 on any error at all. Run diff in the pipeline and accumulated debt stays in the report.

ignore.q: Can I disable a rule on a single page?
ignore.aPost: inside the page. There is no per-URL override anywhere else: set the rule to off in rules, or drop the address from the crawl with crawl.ignore.

playwright.a: The crawler needs it to render pages in Chromium. The Nuxt module and the DevTools tab don't.

price.a: Nothing. Ranklint is entirely free — open source under the MIT license, with no paid tiers and no limits.

cta.title: The next SEO regression won't reach production
cta.lead: Install the module, add two steps to your pipeline — from there the exit code decides.

footer.tagline: An SEO linter for your dev server, your pull requests and production.
